title: Menopause: What to Expect
hook: Menopause isn't a sudden switch. It's a years-long transition with real symptoms and real options to manage them.
key_points: Perimenopause is the lead-up, with changing cycles; menopause is 12 months with no period.
Most people reach menopause between 45 and 55, often around 51.
Common symptoms: hot flashes, night sweats, sleep trouble, mood shifts, vaginal dryness.
Falling estrogen raises long-term risk to bones and the heart.
Options range from lifestyle changes to hormone therapy; discuss the fit with a clinician.
content_html: Menopause is the natural end of menstrual cycles, defined as going 12 months without a period. It rarely arrives overnight. The transition leading up to it, called perimenopause, can last several years as hormones fluctuate and cycles become irregular.
extra_html:
The National Institute on Aging notes that most people reach menopause between ages 45 and 55, often around 51. During the transition, common symptoms include hot flashes, night sweats, trouble sleeping, mood changes, and vaginal dryness. These vary widely; some people barely notice, others find them disruptive.

Because estrogen declines, menopause also raises the long-term risk of bone loss and heart disease, so it's a sensible time to prioritize strength training, calcium and vitamin D, and blood pressure. For bothersome symptoms, the NIA describes a range of options, from lifestyle adjustments to hormone therapy and non-hormonal medicines. The right choice depends on your symptoms and health history, so it's worth a conversation with a clinician.

related.title: The Menstrual Cycle, Explained
related.hook: Your cycle is a monthly report card on your health. Knowing what's normal makes the rare red flag easy to spot.

related.title: Protecting Your Bones
related.hook: Bone looks permanent, but it's living tissue that thins with age. Osteoporosis weakens it silently until a minor fall causes a major break.

related.title: Understanding Blood Pressure
related.hook: High blood pressure is called the 'silent killer' for a reason — it usually has no symptoms, yet it quietly raises your risk of heart attack and stroke.

related.title: Why Regular Checkups Matter
related.hook: The whole point of a checkup is to catch trouble while it's still quiet — before symptoms show up and while it's easiest to treat.

related.title: ADHD Looks Different in Women — and Gets Missed for Decades
related.hook: Girls with ADHD look distracted rather than disruptive, so diagnosis often waits until adulthood. The cost isn't just lost years — one UK study found women with ADHD die nearly nine years earlier.

flashcards.prompt: What technically marks the point of menopause?
flashcards.back_html: Going 12 months in a row without a menstrual period. The years of changing cycles leading up to it are called perimenopause.

flashcards.prompt: Why does menopause matter for long-term health beyond symptoms?

choices.text: Falling estrogen raises risk to bones and the heart
It permanently weakens the immune system
It causes diabetes in most people

flashcards.explanation_html: As estrogen drops, the risk of bone loss (osteoporosis) and heart disease rises, which is why menopause is a good moment to focus on bone and heart health.
